ed-codes-acls-pals-l01.q: A single rescuer is doing CPR on an adult. How long may the compressor spend getting the AED and applying pads before compressions resume?
choices: As long as it takes to get pads placed correctly
Compressions should be interrupted as little as possible; apply pads with minimal pause and resume immediately
Up to 30 seconds is acceptable
Compressions must stop until the AED analyzes
ed-codes-acls-pals-l01.why: Every second off the chest costs pressure that takes multiple compressions to rebuild, so pad placement is done with the shortest possible interruption, ideally while another rescuer compresses. Thirty seconds is far too long, and analysis does not require compressions to have stopped first.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l01.q: During two-rescuer CPR on an adult, what is the correct way to switch compressors?
choices: Stop compressions, switch, then resume within 5 seconds
Switch every 2 minutes during the rhythm check, in under 5 seconds
Switch every time the compressor feels tired, regardless of timing
Switch only after 4 minutes to avoid interrupting flow
ed-codes-acls-pals-l01.why: The 2-minute mark lines up with the rhythm check, which is already a planned pause, so the swap adds no extra interruption if done in under 5 seconds. Waiting for fatigue means quality has already fallen, and 4 minutes is too long between swaps.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l02.q: A patient in VF has received one shock at 150 J on a biphasic device. The rhythm persists. What is a reasonable next energy?
choices: Repeat 150 J only, energy never escalates
200 J, since escalation is reasonable for a refractory rhythm
Drop to 120 J to reduce myocardial injury
Switch immediately to monophasic dosing at 360 J
ed-codes-acls-pals-l02.why: Escalating energy on a biphasic device is reasonable when a shock fails to convert the rhythm. Repeating the same low energy or dropping it further gives the same shock a second chance to fail, and switching device types mid-code is not how escalation works.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l02.q: A patient is found in PEA. IV access is not yet established but an IO is placed within a minute. When should the first epinephrine dose be given?
choices: As soon as the IO is in, since non-shockable rhythms get epinephrine as early as possible
Only after the second rhythm check
Delayed until an IV is obtained instead of the IO
Withheld until the H's and T's are ruled out
ed-codes-acls-pals-l02.why: In non-shockable rhythms, earlier epinephrine correlates with better outcomes, and IO access is an accepted route equivalent to IV for this purpose. Waiting for a rhythm check, a true IV, or a completed differential all needlessly delay the one drug shown to help in this pathway.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l03.q: A trauma patient in PEA has absent breath sounds on the left, jugular venous distension, and the bag feels like it is pushing against a wall. What immediate bedside intervention is indicated?
choices: Pericardiocentesis
Needle or finger decompression of the left chest
Calcium chloride IV
Naloxone 2 mg IN
ed-codes-acls-pals-l03.why: Unilateral absent breath sounds with high ventilation resistance and distended neck veins is tension pneumothorax, treated with decompression on the affected side. Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade, which classically presents with bilateral breath sounds, and calcium and naloxone address unrelated causes.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l03.q: A hypothermic patient at a core temperature of 27 C is found in VF. After one shock the rhythm persists. What is correct?
choices: Continue shocking every 2 minutes and dosing epinephrine on the normal schedule
Limit further shocks and hold repeat drug doses until active rewarming raises the core temperature
Terminate resuscitation immediately since 27 C is below viable threshold
Give double the epinephrine dose to compensate for slow metabolism
ed-codes-acls-pals-l03.why: Below about 30 C the myocardium responds poorly to both shocks and drugs, so further shocks and repeat dosing are limited until rewarming begins — the mnemonic is not dead until warm and dead. Standard dosing intervals, immediate termination, and dose-doubling are all wrong for this physiology.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l04.q: Two rescuers are bagging an adult with a bag-valve mask before an advanced airway is placed. What is the correct division of labor and volume target?
choices: One person holds the seal with both hands while the other squeezes to visible chest rise, about 500 to 600 mL
One person does both seal and squeeze alone for consistency
Both rescuers alternate squeezing every other breath
The seal is held with one hand so the other hand can manage the oxygen tubing
ed-codes-acls-pals-l04.why: A two-hand seal by one rescuer prevents the leak that a one-handed seal produces, while the second rescuer squeezes to just visible chest rise. Alternating squeezers or freeing a hand for tubing both reintroduce the single-hand seal problem.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l04.q: Immediately after ROSC, the patient is still being bagged at a high rate out of habit from the code. What should change about oxygen delivery right away?
choices: Nothing changes until the patient reaches the ICU
Titrate down to target SpO2 92 to 98% instead of maximal oxygen
Switch to room air immediately
Increase the rate further to wash out accumulated CO2
ed-codes-acls-pals-l04.why: The moment there is a pulse, maximal oxygen becomes harmful because it generates free radicals in reperfused tissue, so it is titrated to 92 to 98%. Waiting until the ICU, jumping straight to room air, or increasing the rate all ignore the immediate post-ROSC change in target.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l05.q: A heart transplant recipient develops symptomatic bradycardia. Atropine 1 mg is given with no effect. Why, and what is next?
choices: The dose was too low; repeat at 2 mg
A transplanted heart has no vagal innervation, so atropine cannot work — move to pacing or an infusion
Atropine takes longer to act in transplant patients; wait 10 minutes
Atropine is contraindicated in transplant patients and should never have been given
ed-codes-acls-pals-l05.why: Atropine works by blocking vagal tone on the sinus node, and a transplanted heart is surgically denervated, so there is no vagal brake to block. It was reasonable to try since it is fast and low-risk, but the correct next step is pacing or an infusion, not a higher dose or a wait.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l05.q: A patient with symptomatic bradycardia has a Mobitz type II block. Atropine is given while pacing and sedation are prepared in parallel. Why prepare pacing before knowing whether atropine worked?
choices: Because atropine is expected to fail in high-grade block, so waiting to prepare after the fact costs minutes
Because atropine always fails and should not have been given at all
Because pacing must be started before any drug is given
Because preparation has no time benefit either way
ed-codes-acls-pals-l05.why: High-grade block sits below the AV node where atropine has little effect, so preparing the next step in parallel avoids losing minutes if the drug fails, which it usually does. Atropine is still reasonable to try briefly since it is fast and harmless, and pacing does not have to precede it.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l06.q: A patient is receiving a procainamide infusion for stable wide complex tachycardia. Which finding should stop the infusion?
choices: The QRS widens by more than 50% from baseline
The heart rate drops below 100
The infusion has run for exactly 5 minutes
The patient reports mild lightheadedness
ed-codes-acls-pals-l06.why: Procainamide is stopped for conversion, hypotension, QRS widening beyond 50%, or reaching 17 mg/kg — QRS widening signals sodium channel toxicity. A falling rate toward normal, a fixed time point, or mild lightheadedness alone are not stopping criteria by themselves.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l06.q: A stable patient in narrow-complex SVT does not convert with a modified Valsalva. Adenosine 6 mg is given but fails. What is the next step?
choices: Repeat 6 mg exactly as given the first time
Give a second dose of adenosine 12 mg
Move directly to synchronized cardioversion since the patient is stable
Switch immediately to procainamide
ed-codes-acls-pals-l06.why: The adenosine sequence is 6 mg then 12 mg if the first dose fails, still as a rapid push with an immediate flush. Repeating the same low dose wastes the second attempt, cardioversion is reserved for instability, and procainamide is the pathway for wide-complex rhythms.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l07.q: A post-ROSC patient is being ventilated and the capnography reads a PaCO2 of 24 mmHg on arterial blood gas. What should change?
choices: Nothing; a low PaCO2 is protective for the brain after arrest
Decrease the ventilation rate to bring PaCO2 toward the normal 35 to 45 mmHg range
Increase the ventilation rate further to fully normalize oxygenation
Switch to bag-valve-mask ventilation instead of a ventilator
ed-codes-acls-pals-l07.why: Post-arrest care targets a normal PaCO2 of roughly 35 to 45 mmHg; hyperventilation to a lower number reduces cerebral blood flow at exactly the wrong time. It is not protective, increasing the rate further worsens the problem, and the delivery device is not the issue here.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l07.q: A patient remains comatose 6 hours after ROSC and cooling has been initiated. The family asks whether the patient will wake up. What is the appropriate response regarding prognosis?
choices: A definitive prognosis can be given now based on the exam
Prognostication is deferred, usually to at least 72 hours after normothermia, since sedation and cooling suppress the exam
The patient will not recover since they remain comatose this early
Prognosis should be based solely on the initial rhythm
ed-codes-acls-pals-l07.why: Sedation, paralytics and therapeutic temperature management all mask the neurologic exam in the first hours to days, so meaningful prognostication waits until at least 72 hours after normothermia. Giving a definitive answer either way this early is not supported, and initial rhythm alone does not determine prognosis.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l08.q: The recorder announces that 4 minutes have passed since the last epinephrine dose. What is this an example of?
choices: An unnecessary interruption that should be saved for the debrief
The recorder's job of tracking drug and rhythm-check intervals and calling them out to the team
A duplicate of the leader's job and therefore redundant
Something only the team leader is permitted to track
ed-codes-acls-pals-l08.why: Tracking the 2-minute rhythm-check interval and drug timing is specifically the recorder's role, and calling it out loud is what keeps the team from missing a dose or a check. It is not redundant with the leader, who is managing decisions rather than the clock, and it should not be saved for later.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l08.q: A code has been running for 10 minutes and the team needs two more units of blood and a specific antidote from pharmacy. Whose job is it to retrieve these?
choices: The team leader, who should leave the room to get them
The runner, freeing everyone else to stay on their assigned task
The recorder, in addition to timing duties
Whoever is standing nearest the door at the time
ed-codes-acls-pals-l08.why: The runner role exists specifically so blood bank, pharmacy, lab, and extra equipment requests do not pull a hands-on team member — often the tech — away from compressions, airway, or access. The leader stays to direct the algorithm, and an ad hoc assignment risks nobody actually going.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l09.q: A tech opens the crash cart and finds the breakaway lock number does not match the log. What should happen?
choices: Use the cart as normal since a mismatched number is usually clerical error
Treat the cart as unverified and check its contents before relying on it in a code
Replace only the defibrillator, since that is the most critical item
Wait until after the next code to investigate
ed-codes-acls-pals-l09.why: A mismatched lock number is the classic sign of a broken seal from a prior partial use, meaning contents may be missing or expired, so the cart must be checked rather than trusted. Assuming clerical error, checking only one item, or deferring the check all risk discovering a missing supply mid-code.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l09.q: An IO is being placed in a 6 kg infant. Which needle size is correct?
choices: 15 mm pink, sized for 3 to 39 kg
25 mm blue, sized for 40 kg and up
45 mm yellow, sized for the humerus or heavy tissue
Any size works equally well in an infant
ed-codes-acls-pals-l09.why: The 15 mm pink needle covers the 3 to 39 kg range, which includes a 6 kg infant. The 25 mm blue needle is for patients 40 kg and up, the 45 mm yellow is for the humerus or heavy tissue, and needle size is weight- and site-dependent, not interchangeable.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l10.q: A 5-year-old has a narrow complex tachycardia at 195 that varies slightly with activity, with visible P waves. Does this meet the pattern for SVT?
choices: Yes, any rate above 180 in a child is SVT
No — SVT is suspected above roughly 180 in a child with a rate that does not vary with activity and no visible P waves; this rhythm has both P waves and rate variability
Yes, because the child is symptomatic
No, because SVT never occurs in children this age
ed-codes-acls-pals-l10.why: The distinguishing features of pediatric SVT are a fixed rate that does not vary with activity and absent P waves — this rhythm has visible P waves and some rate variability, both more consistent with sinus tachycardia. Rate alone above 180 is not sufficient, and SVT does occur at this age.

ed-codes-acls-pals-l10.q: A term newborn is being resuscitated and preductal saturation needs to be monitored. Where is the pulse oximeter placed?
choices: The left hand
The right hand
Either foot
The earlobe
ed-codes-acls-pals-l10.why: Preductal saturation reflects blood that has not yet passed the ductus arteriosus, and the right hand receives preductal flow via the right subclavian artery, which is why it is the standard site. The left hand and the feet are postductal or mixed, and the earlobe is not a newborn monitoring site.

quiz.q: A lone rescuer finds an adult collapsed and unresponsive with no normal breathing. After confirming no pulse in under 10 seconds, what is the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio?
choices: Compressions only, no ventilation ever
quiz.why: A single rescuer on an adult uses 30:2 regardless of age-specific pediatric ratios. 15:2 applies to two-rescuer pediatric CPR, 5:1 is not a recognized ratio, and ventilation is part of standard CPR unless the rescuer is untrained and doing compression-only CPR by choice.

quiz.q: During CPR on a 9-year-old, the rescuer is compressing to a depth of about 1.5 inches. What is the correction?
choices: That depth is correct for this age
Depth should be about 2 inches or one third of chest depth for a child this age
Depth should match the infant standard of 1.5 inches since the child is small
Depth is irrelevant as long as the rate is 100 to 120
quiz.why: A 9-year-old falls in the child category (1 year to puberty), where depth is about 2 inches or one third of chest depth — 1.5 inches is the infant target. Rate matters, but depth is not irrelevant; both drive coronary perfusion pressure together.

quiz.q: A rescuer leans on the chest between compressions without realizing it. What physiologic effect does this have?
choices: It only matters if compressions are also too shallow
It increases coronary perfusion pressure
It prevents the chest from fully recoiling, blocking venous return during the filling phase
It has no measurable hemodynamic effect
quiz.why: Recoil is the filling phase of the compression cycle; leaning keeps intrathoracic pressure elevated and blood cannot return to fill the heart before the next compression. It does not raise perfusion pressure, and the effect is present independent of depth.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old, roughly 22 kg, needs defibrillation and the department's only pads are adult pads with no pediatric attenuator available. What should the team do?
choices: Cut the adult pads down to a smaller size
Wait for pediatric pads to arrive from another unit
Withhold defibrillation and continue CPR only
Use the adult pads rather than withhold a shock
quiz.why: An imperfect shock with adult pads is far better than no shock at all in a shockable pediatric rhythm. Withholding defibrillation or waiting for equipment to arrive sacrifices the single intervention proven to help, and cutting pads is not a supported modification.

quiz.q: A team is asked what chest compression fraction they should aim for during a code. What is the correct target range?
choices: At least 60%, with good teams reaching 80%
Exactly 50%, no higher or lower
100%, meaning no pauses of any kind
At least 40%, with 60% considered excellent
quiz.why: Sixty percent is the floor and eighty percent reflects a well-run code; some pause is unavoidable for rhythm checks and shocks, so 100% is not realistic. A 40% floor or a rigid 50% target both undersell what quality CPR requires.

quiz.q: A patient is in refractory VF. The team has given amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock and the rhythm persists after a fourth shock. What is the correct next amiodarone dose if repeated?
choices: 300 mg again
150 mg
600 mg
Amiodarone is not repeated under any circumstance
quiz.why: The second amiodarone dose, if needed, is 150 mg rather than repeating the full 300 mg loading dose. Six hundred milligrams exceeds the protocol, and the drug is designed to be repeatable once for a persistently refractory rhythm.

quiz.q: A patient's arrest rhythm converts from VF to organized complexes with a palpable pulse mid-cycle, discovered at the next scheduled rhythm check. What determines whether the team continues to the shockable or non-shockable pathway?
choices: Pathway is determined only by total elapsed time
The pathway is fixed by the initial rhythm and never changes
The current rhythm and pulse status at each check determine the path going forward — this patient has achieved ROSC and moves to post-arrest care
The team must complete at least 3 shocks before reassessing pathway
quiz.why: Each rhythm check re-evaluates the current state; a pulse with an organized rhythm means ROSC and a shift to post-arrest care regardless of the initial rhythm. The pathway is not locked at the start, nor gated by a shock count or a time threshold.

quiz.q: A monophasic defibrillator is the only unit available for an adult in VF. What energy should be used?
quiz.why: Monophasic defibrillation uses 360 J, higher than the 120 to 200 J biphasic range because monophasic waveforms are less efficient at delivering current. The other values are biphasic or cardioversion energies, not the monophasic defibrillation dose.

quiz.q: A code has been running for 12 minutes in asystole with no reversible cause identified. Which drug should NOT be given routinely at this point?
choices: Sodium bicarbonate, unless a specific indication like hyperkalemia is present
Continued CPR
Reassessment for H's and T's
Epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes
quiz.why: Bicarbonate is reserved for specific causes, not given routinely for prolonged downtime or presumed acidosis alone. Epinephrine, ongoing CPR, and reassessing for reversible causes all remain appropriate and expected throughout the code.

quiz.q: A code leader wants to confirm true asystole rather than fine VF on the monitor. What three checks should be done before accepting the flat-line reading?
choices: Check the patient's age, weight, and downtime
Check lead connections, gain setting, and the rhythm in a second lead
Check the IV site, the oxygen flow, and the backboard placement
Check the epinephrine dose, the last shock time, and the compressor's fatigue level
quiz.why: Fine VF can appear flat with a loose lead or low gain and is shockable, so leads, gain, and a second lead view are checked before calling asystole. The other option sets are unrelated to distinguishing a true flat line from fine VF.

quiz.q: A patient arrests from a witnessed massive GI hemorrhage. The monitor shows a fast, narrow-complex PEA. Which H is most likely, and what is the priority action?
choices: Hyperkalemia — give calcium
Hypothermia — begin active rewarming
Hypovolemia — give blood and fluids rapidly
Hydrogen ion — give bicarbonate
quiz.why: A witnessed hemorrhage with fast narrow-complex PEA points directly to hypovolemia, treated with rapid volume and blood replacement rather than a metabolic or thermal intervention. Fast narrow-complex PEA fits volume-related or mechanical causes, not slow wide-complex metabolic ones.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has known end-stage renal disease and last dialyzed 4 days ago. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Besides calcium, which two treatments target the underlying cause?
choices: Magnesium and procainamide
Atropine and pacing
Naloxone and epinephrine
Bicarbonate and insulin with dextrose
quiz.why: Hyperkalemia is treated with calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane plus bicarbonate and insulin-dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly. The other drug pairs treat opioid overdose, torsades or wide-complex tachycardia, and bradycardia, none of which is the primary problem here.

quiz.q: A patient found unresponsive next to empty pill bottles arrests with a known history of tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Which specific treatment is indicated beyond standard ACLS?
choices: Sodium bicarbonate for sodium-channel blockade
Atropine 1 mg
Magnesium sulfate 4 g
Naloxone 2 mg
quiz.why: Tricyclic overdose causes sodium-channel blockade, and bicarbonate is a specific antidote that narrows the QRS and reduces arrhythmia risk. Naloxone treats opioids, atropine has no arrest role, and magnesium is not the specific antidote for this toxin.

quiz.q: A near-drowning victim is found pulseless after being submerged for an unknown time. Compared to a typical adult cardiac arrest, what should change about initial management?
choices: Skip ventilation and focus solely on compressions since drowning is a cardiac event
Prioritize early rescue breaths since drowning arrest is primarily hypoxic
Give epinephrine before starting any compressions
Withhold resuscitation given the presumed downtime
quiz.why: Drowning arrest results from hypoxia, so ventilation is prioritized rather than defaulting to compression-only CPR as might be reasonable in a witnessed primary cardiac arrest. Skipping ventilation, delaying compressions for a drug, or withholding care outright all misread the mechanism.

quiz.q: A 26-week pregnant patient arrests. The uterus is palpated at the level of the umbilicus. What intervention is required for the duration of the code?
choices: Positioning the patient fully on her right side
Elevate the legs 30 degrees
Continuous manual left uterine displacement by a dedicated team member
Immediate cesarean delivery regardless of downtime
quiz.why: A uterus at or above the navel compresses the vena cava, so continuous manual left displacement is required throughout, keeping the chest flat for effective compressions. Right-sided positioning would worsen rather than relieve compression, leg elevation does not address it, and immediate delivery is not the first step — it is considered at 4 minutes if there is no ROSC.

quiz.q: A patient in anaphylaxis develops hypotension and stridor. What is the correct epinephrine dose, route, and site?
choices: 1 mg intramuscular into the deltoid
0.1 mg subcutaneous into the abdomen
0.3 to 0.5 mg IV push
0.3 to 0.5 mg intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh
quiz.why: Anaphylaxis epinephrine is 0.3 to 0.5 mg intramuscular into the thigh, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes — the thigh has better absorption than the deltoid, and IV push at this dose risks dangerous arrhythmia. Subcutaneous administration is also not the recommended route for anaphylaxis.

quiz.q: A patient arrests after a stab wound to the chest. Compressions are started immediately. What should the team prioritize alongside or instead of prolonged compressions?
choices: Controlling hemorrhage, decompressing both sides of the chest, and giving blood
Giving a full dose of epinephrine before any procedural intervention
Waiting for a full trauma team before doing anything
Continuing compressions exactly as in a medical arrest, since the algorithm is identical
quiz.why: Traumatic arrest is addressed by fixing the mechanical and hemorrhagic cause, since compressions on an empty, non-filling heart accomplish little. Treating it identically to a medical arrest, prioritizing a drug over the cause, or delaying for more staff all cost time the patient does not have.

quiz.q: A patient is being bagged with a bag-valve mask before intubation. The rescuer is squeezing hard and fast, causing visible chest rise well beyond normal. What is the risk?
choices: Improved oxygenation with no downside
Increased intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return and lowering survival
Gastric distension only, with no cardiovascular effect
Faster CO2 clearance improving capnography readings
quiz.why: Excessive volume and rate raise intrathoracic pressure, which impairs venous return and directly lowers survival — this is the core hazard of hyperventilation during CPR. Gastric distension is a real side effect but not the primary hemodynamic concern, and CO2 clearance changes do not offset the harm.

quiz.q: An unresponsive adult needs an oral airway. How should it be sized?
choices: One size fits all adults
From the earlobe to the tip of the nose
From the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
From the corner of the mouth to the sternal notch
quiz.why: Oral airways are sized from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw (or sometimes the earlobe as a landmark), which approximates the distance needed to clear the tongue from the airway. The sternal notch and nose-to-ear measurements are not the standard landmarks, and sizing does vary by patient.

quiz.q: A patient has an advanced airway in place during a code, and ventilation is being delivered every 3 seconds instead of every 6. What is the consequence?
choices: No effect since an advanced airway allows any rate
Better waveform capnography readings
Improved oxygenation with no downside
Hyperventilation, which raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return
quiz.why: Even with an advanced airway, the correct rate is 10 breaths per minute (one every 6 seconds); doubling that rate reintroduces the hyperventilation problem the continuous-compression strategy is designed to avoid. An advanced airway changes the compression pattern, not the ventilation rate ceiling.

quiz.q: During CPR, the waveform capnography shows a consistent value of 34 mmHg over several breaths with a normal-appearing waveform shape. What does this confirm?
choices: The tube is correctly placed in the trachea and ventilating
ROSC has occurred
Compressions are inadequate
The tube is in the esophagus
quiz.why: A persistent, sustained waveform over multiple breaths confirms tracheal placement — esophageal placement produces no sustained waveform at all. A value of 34 is not the sudden rise above 35 to 40 that signals ROSC, and this value does not indicate inadequate compressions, which is a concern under 10 mmHg.

quiz.q: A team has been compressing for 22 minutes on an intubated patient with persistent ETCO2 readings of 6 to 8 mmHg despite good technique. What does this suggest?
choices: The tube has become dislodged
A very poor prognosis, though it remains one input to the leader's decision, not the sole reason to stop
The patient needs immediate cardioversion
Epinephrine dosing has been too infrequent
quiz.why: Persistently low ETCO2 despite good CPR after 20 minutes correlates with poor outcome and is factored into termination decisions, but it is not by itself grounds to stop — other factors like reversible causes and rhythm still matter. A dislodged tube would produce no waveform at all, cardioversion is irrelevant to a persistently low reading, and the scenario states technique is already good.

quiz.q: A patient is being bagged before intubation and capnography reads 4 mmHg with no discernible waveform shape at all despite good-looking chest rise. What should be suspected?
choices: Normal readings for this stage of the code
Excellent compression quality
Possible esophageal or displaced airway placement, or a disconnected circuit, requiring immediate reassessment
Impending ROSC
quiz.why: A flat trace with no waveform shape, as opposed to a low but present waveform, raises concern for a disconnected or misplaced airway device and needs immediate reassessment of the airway and circuit. A low but shaped waveform reflects compression quality; a flat trace with no shape reflects a technical or placement problem instead.

quiz.q: A patient has a heart rate of 38 but is asymptomatic, alert, and hemodynamically normal. According to the bradycardia algorithm, what is the correct action?
choices: Begin transcutaneous pacing as a precaution
Start a dopamine infusion
Atropine 1 mg IV immediately
Monitor, obtain IV access and a 12-lead, and look for a cause without treating the rate itself
quiz.why: Treatment is triggered by symptoms — hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, or heart failure — not by the number alone, so an asymptomatic patient is monitored and worked up rather than treated. Atropine, pacing, and infusions all carry risk without a clear benefit here.

quiz.q: A symptomatic bradycardic patient has received atropine 1 mg, then 1 mg again 4 minutes later, for a running total of 2 mg, with no improvement. What is correct regarding further atropine?
choices: One more 1 mg dose may be given to reach the 3 mg maximum, while pacing or an infusion is prepared in parallel
No further atropine may be given under any circumstance
The next dose must be doubled to 2 mg
Atropine should be switched to an IM route for faster onset
quiz.why: The maximum total is 3 mg, so one more 1 mg dose is within protocol, but since two doses have already failed, pacing or a vasopressor infusion should be prepared simultaneously rather than waiting on a third dose alone. Doubling the dose and switching routes are not part of the standard protocol.

quiz.q: Transcutaneous pacing is started on a symptomatic bradycardic patient without any sedation because the team is in a hurry. What is the concern?
choices: Pacing is painless so sedation is unnecessary
Pacing is genuinely painful and an awake patient will not tolerate it without sedation and analgesia
Sedation would prevent capture from being detected
Sedation is only needed for cardioversion, not pacing
quiz.why: Transcutaneous pacing delivers a strong electrical impulse through the chest wall, which is uncomfortable to the point that patients need sedation and analgesia to tolerate it. Sedation does not interfere with capture assessment, and pacing is at least as painful as cardioversion, not exempt from the need for comfort measures.

quiz.q: During transcutaneous pacing, the team increases the milliamp output slowly from a low starting point rather than starting at maximum. Why?
choices: It does not matter; either approach works identically
Starting low prevents electrical capture entirely
Starting low finds the capture threshold with less pain than starting at maximum
Starting at maximum output damages the pacer
quiz.why: Raising output gradually from a low starting point identifies the minimum current needed for capture while minimizing the patient's pain, rather than immediately delivering a painful maximum-output current. It does not damage the device to start high, nor does starting low prevent capture — it simply reaches it more gently.

quiz.q: A patient with symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension is started on a dopamine infusion instead of pacing. What dose range is correct?
choices: 2 to 10 mcg/min
50 to 100 mcg/kg/min
0.1 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min
5 to 20 mcg/kg/min
quiz.why: Dopamine for symptomatic bradycardia runs at 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min. The 0.1 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min range is norepinephrine's post-arrest dosing, 2 to 10 mcg/min is the epinephrine infusion range, and 50 to 100 mcg/kg/min is far above any standard infusion dose.

quiz.q: A patient has an inferior wall myocardial infarction and develops new bradycardia with a systolic of 82 and dizziness. What is the likely mechanism?
choices: The artery supplying the inferior wall also supplies the AV node, so the infarction can produce bradycardia or heart block
Excess atropine given prehospital
A vagal response to pain medication only
Coincidental unrelated conduction disease
quiz.why: The right coronary artery, which frequently supplies both the inferior wall and the AV node, explains why inferior MI is classically associated with bradyarrhythmias and heart block. This is not coincidental, and while pain and vagal tone can contribute, the anatomic link to the AV node's blood supply is the key mechanism being tested here.

quiz.q: A patient with new atrial fibrillation at 172 has a blood pressure of 68/40 and is confused. What is the correct immediate treatment?
choices: Adenosine 6 mg rapid push
Synchronized cardioversion at 120 to 200 J
Metoprolol 5 mg IV and reassess in 20 minutes
Vagal maneuvers first, then reassess
quiz.why: This patient is unstable — hypotensive and confused — so synchronized cardioversion at the narrow-irregular dose of 120 to 200 J is indicated rather than a drug trial. Adenosine does not reliably convert atrial fibrillation, and beta blockers or vagal maneuvers are appropriate only for the stable patient, which this one is not.

quiz.q: A patient is in stable, regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 160. Under what condition might adenosine be considered?
choices: Only if the rhythm is known to be VT with certainty
Adenosine should never be given to any wide-complex tachycardia
It may be considered specifically because the rhythm is regular and monomorphic
It is preferred over procainamide for all wide-complex tachycardias
quiz.why: Adenosine may be considered in a stable wide-complex tachycardia only when it is regular and monomorphic, since this profile is the one where a reentrant SVT with aberrancy is a realistic possibility. It is not the preferred first-line drug over an antiarrhythmic infusion, and it is not given for irregular or polymorphic wide-complex rhythms.

quiz.q: A patient in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia loses pulses. What is the correct next step?
choices: Adenosine 6 mg immediately
Amiodarone 300 mg IV, holding the defibrillator
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
Unsynchronized defibrillation, following the VF/pulseless VT pathway
quiz.why: A pulseless patient in any rhythm, including polymorphic VT, is treated with the cardiac arrest algorithm — CPR and unsynchronized defibrillation — rather than a pulse-present tachycardia pathway. Synchronized cardioversion and adenosine assume a pulse, and holding the defibrillator to give a drug first delays the one definitive treatment.

quiz.q: A patient develops torsades de pointes with a pulse and a blood pressure of 100/60. What should be checked or corrected alongside giving magnesium?
choices: Contributing electrolyte abnormalities such as low potassium and any QT-prolonging medications
The patient's baseline heart rate from a year ago
Whether the patient has ever had a normal ECG
Nothing further is needed once magnesium is given
quiz.why: Torsades is often driven or worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or QT-prolonging drugs, so correcting these alongside magnesium addresses the underlying driver rather than only the acute rhythm. A prior year-old ECG or a one-time normal tracing does not change the current management.

quiz.q: A patient with SVT converts after adenosine 6 mg, but the team notices the rhythm strip briefly showed flutter waves during the few seconds of AV block before conversion. What does this illustrate about adenosine?
choices: Adenosine only works by directly terminating flutter
Even when it does not convert a rhythm, the brief AV block from adenosine can unmask underlying atrial activity like flutter waves
The flutter waves indicate the adenosine dose was too low
This is an adverse reaction requiring atropine
quiz.why: Adenosine's brief AV nodal block can reveal underlying atrial activity such as flutter waves even when it does not terminate the tachycardia itself, which is diagnostically useful and expected. It is not evidence of underdosing or an adverse reaction requiring atropine.

quiz.q: Ten minutes after ROSC, the patient's blood pressure is 108/68 and SpO2 is 96% on titrated oxygen. What should happen regarding the 12-lead ECG?
choices: It should only be obtained if the patient reports chest pain
It can wait until the patient is admitted to the ICU
It should be obtained as soon as possible, since a large share of adult arrests are caused by coronary occlusion
It is unnecessary since the patient is hemodynamically stable
quiz.why: The 12-lead is obtained as soon as possible after ROSC regardless of hemodynamic stability or symptoms, because it routes the patient to the cath lab if a coronary cause is found — and a comatose or sedated patient cannot report chest pain even when present. Waiting for ICU admission or symptom report both risk delaying definitive treatment.

quiz.q: A post-ROSC patient's blood pressure drifts to 84/50 once, then normalizes on its own without intervention over the next 10 minutes. How should this be regarded?
choices: As proof that no vasopressor will ever be needed
As a normal and expected part of the post-arrest course requiring no documentation
As clinically insignificant since it resolved on its own
As an event that independently worsens survival and neurologic outcome, even though it self-resolved, and should prompt closer monitoring and readiness to intervene
quiz.why: Even a single episode of post-arrest hypotension is independently associated with worse outcomes, so it is treated as clinically significant and documented, with heightened vigilance for recurrence, even if it resolves before intervention. It is not something to dismiss, assume will never recur, or leave undocumented.

quiz.q: A comatose post-arrest patient is started on targeted temperature management. What is the most important underlying principle of the therapy?
choices: Selecting and maintaining a constant temperature between 32 and 37.5 C and avoiding fever, more than hitting one specific number
Cooling as low as tolerated for maximum neuroprotection
Temperature control is optional if the patient is hemodynamically stable
Reaching exactly 33 C is the only acceptable target
quiz.why: Current guidance emphasizes deliberate, constant temperature control within a 32 to 37.5 C range and preventing fever, rather than any single mandatory target number, and deeper cooling has not shown added benefit. It applies based on failing to follow commands, not hemodynamic status, and is not optional in that population.

quiz.q: A post-arrest patient's glucose returns at 52 mg/dL. What should the team do?
choices: Ignore it since glucose is not part of post-arrest care
Treat the hypoglycemia, since checking and correcting glucose is part of standard post-arrest management
Wait until temperature management is complete before addressing it
Only treat if the patient is symptomatic
quiz.why: Glucose is checked and hypoglycemia treated as part of the everything-else bundle of post-arrest care, alongside the 12-lead, blood pressure, and oxygenation targets — a comatose patient cannot report hypoglycemic symptoms. Waiting for cooling to finish or ignoring it both risk ongoing neuronal injury from unrecognized hypoglycemia.

quiz.q: A post-arrest patient remains comatose and is placed on continuous EEG monitoring. What is the primary reason for this?
choices: To determine the initial arrest rhythm retrospectively
To confirm brain death immediately
Because seizures after arrest are common and often clinically invisible without EEG
Because EEG is required before starting temperature management
quiz.why: Post-arrest seizures frequently occur without visible motor signs, so continuous EEG is used to detect them in a comatose patient who cannot otherwise show clinical evidence. EEG does not determine the original arrest rhythm, is not a prerequisite for starting cooling, and is not used to declare brain death this early.

quiz.q: During a code, the physician says "someone get an amp of bicarb" without naming anyone. Two techs both start looking for it, unsure if the other is handling it. What breakdown does this illustrate?
choices: An appropriate use of the runner role
A properly executed repeat-back
Correct use of closed-loop communication
A released order with no named recipient, the classic cause of confusion, duplication, or a missed task
quiz.why: An order given to the room rather than to a named person is exactly the failure mode that leads to duplicated effort or a dropped task, as described in the closed-loop communication principle. It is the opposite of closed-loop communication and does not involve a repeat-back or a designated runner task.

quiz.q: A tech is assigned as both compressor and airway assistant in a short-staffed code. What is the correct approach to this dual assignment?
choices: Accept it, since small departments legitimately combine roles, but both roles must still be clearly acknowledged and named
Perform only the role assigned first and ignore the second
Assign the second role silently to another team member without telling the leader
Refuse the second role since roles must never be combined
quiz.why: The material explicitly allows combining roles in smaller teams as long as everyone, including the person holding them, knows which roles are covered — silent reassignment or outright refusal both break the clarity the system depends on. Ignoring one of the two roles leaves a gap nobody is covering.

quiz.q: A team leader asks the room if anyone has another idea before terminating a resuscitation. A tech recalls the patient has a fistula suggesting dialysis dependence, not yet mentioned. What should the tech do?
choices: Stay silent since this is the physician's decision alone
Speak up with the observation, since termination decisions benefit from any relevant fact a team member has noticed
Wait until after the code ends to mention it in the debrief
Assume someone else has already considered it
quiz.why: The leader's invitation for other ideas exists precisely because any team member may hold a fact that changes the differential, such as a fistula suggesting missed dialysis and hyperkalemia. Staying silent, waiting for the debrief, or assuming it has been considered all risk losing a treatable cause at the critical moment.

quiz.q: A resuscitation is ongoing and the patient's spouse is in the waiting room, distraught. No staff member has been assigned to them yet. What should happen before offering the spouse the option to be present at the bedside?
choices: Have the recorder handle both timing duties and the spouse simultaneously
Bring the spouse in immediately regardless of staffing
Assign a dedicated staff member to stay with, explain to, and if needed escort the spouse before offering bedside presence
Wait until the code ends to speak with the spouse at all
quiz.why: Family presence is supported specifically when one person is dedicated solely to that role; bringing someone in unsupported, or combining that duty with an already-demanding recorder role, undermines the support the evidence depends on. Waiting until the code ends entirely is also not what the guidance recommends when presence is being considered.

quiz.q: After a code ends, the team holds a short debrief. A tech noticed the defibrillator pads would not stick properly and had to be replaced mid-code, costing time. What should the tech do?
choices: Wait to see if anyone else brings it up first
File a formal complaint instead of mentioning it in debrief
Say nothing since the outcome was ultimately fine
Report the observation during the debrief as a concrete finding for the next code
quiz.why: The debrief is specifically the place for concrete, practical findings like faulty pads — often something only the tech in that role would have noticed — and voicing it improves the next code. Staying silent or waiting for someone else to raise it risks the issue recurring, and a formal complaint is not the appropriate channel for equipment feedback meant to improve practice.

quiz.q: A patient needs anterior-posterior pad placement for pacing. Where do the two pads go?
choices: One on the anterior chest, one between the shoulder blades on the back
Both on the back, at the level of the scapulae
One on the abdomen, one on the anterior chest
Both on the anterior chest, side by side
quiz.why: Anterior-posterior placement puts one pad on the chest and one between the shoulder blades, which is preferred for pacing, atrial fibrillation cardioversion, and infants. Placing both pads on the same surface does not create the current pathway through the heart that this configuration is designed for.

quiz.q: A patient arriving for defibrillation has a nitroglycerin patch on the chest directly under where a pad needs to go. What should be done?
choices: Place the pad directly over the patch since timing matters more
Remove the patch and wipe the skin before placing the pad
Move the pad only 1 cm to the side of the patch without removing it
Cardioversion cannot proceed until the patch has been on for at least an hour
quiz.why: A medication patch under a pad can arc and cause a burn or interfere with current delivery, so it is removed and the skin wiped clean before pad placement. Placing the pad over it or barely shifting position both risk the arcing hazard, and there is no time-based waiting requirement described.

quiz.q: A team delivers a shock and immediately calls out the clear sequence, but oxygen is still flowing across the patient's chest from an open mask during the shock. What is the concern?
choices: It will interfere with rhythm interpretation
Oxygen flow has no relevance to defibrillation safety
Flowing oxygen across the chest during a shock is a fire risk
It will falsely lower the delivered energy
quiz.why: Flowing oxygen near a spark from the shock is a real fire hazard, which is why the clear sequence explicitly includes confirming oxygen is directed away even though the bag itself stays connected to the tube. It does not change delivered energy or rhythm interpretation — the concern is purely a fire safety one.

quiz.q: A team successfully cardioverts a patient in atrial flutter with sync mode. The rhythm reverts a minute later and a second cardioversion is planned. What must be rechecked before the second shock?
choices: That the pads have been repositioned to a new location
That the patient has been re-consented
Nothing — sync mode remains engaged from the first shock
That sync mode is selected again, since most defibrillators default back to unsynchronized after a discharge
quiz.why: Most defibrillators automatically revert to unsynchronized mode after each discharge, so failing to reselect sync before a second cardioversion risks an unsynchronized shock landing on a vulnerable T wave. Pads generally do not need repositioning between consecutive shocks, and re-consenting is not a device safety step.

quiz.q: An adult patient needs IO access and the proximal humerus is chosen because faster flow is needed. What is the tradeoff of this site compared to the tibia?
choices: The humerus flows fastest but dislodges more easily with arm movement
The humerus cannot accept the same medications as the tibia
The humerus requires a smaller needle regardless of patient size
The humerus has no tradeoff and is always superior
quiz.why: The humerus offers the fastest flow and quickest drug delivery of the standard IO sites but is more prone to dislodging if the arm moves, which is the tradeoff against its speed advantage. It accepts the same range of medications as other IO sites, and needle size is based on weight and tissue depth, not simply the chosen site.

quiz.q: A tibial IO was placed in a patient 30 hours ago for a prior resuscitation and has since been removed. The same leg's tibia is now being considered for a new IO. Is this an acceptable site?
choices: Yes, since the prior IO has already been removed
No, a bone with an IO placed within the last 48 hours should not be reused
Yes, as long as a smaller needle is used
No, that bone can never be used again for the rest of the patient's life
quiz.why: The 48-hour rule excludes reusing a bone regardless of whether the prior device has been removed, since the prior insertion site can leak infusate. It is not a permanent lifetime exclusion, and using a smaller needle does not address the leakage risk from the recent puncture.

quiz.q: A 25 kg 6-year-old is in pulseless VT. After the first shock at 2 J/kg fails to convert, what is the correct energy for the second shock?
quiz.why: The second pediatric shock is 4 J/kg: 4 x 25 = 100 J. Fifty joules would only be 2 J/kg (the first-shock dose), and 150 J and 25 J do not correspond to the weight-based algorithm at this step.

quiz.q: A 20 kg child in cardiac arrest needs amiodarone for shock-refractory VF. What is the correct dose?
choices: 300 mg, the fixed adult dose
5 mg total, regardless of weight
20 mg
100 mg
quiz.why: Pediatric amiodarone is 5 mg/kg, so 5 x 20 = 100 mg, repeatable up to two more times. The fixed adult 300 mg dose does not apply to a weight-based pediatric patient, and 20 mg and 5 mg total both far underdose a 20 kg child.

quiz.q: A newborn is 20 seconds old, blue, and not breathing. The team has already dried and stimulated with no response. What should happen next, and within what time frame?
choices: Position the airway and prepare to begin positive-pressure ventilation if the heart rate is under 100 or there is apnea, aiming to start within the first 60 seconds of life
Begin chest compressions immediately since the newborn is not breathing
Give epinephrine via the umbilical vein now
Continue drying and stimulating for a full 60 seconds before reassessing
quiz.why: The newborn algorithm calls for positive-pressure ventilation within the first 60 seconds ('the golden minute') if apneic or heart rate is under 100, after initial drying, stimulation, and airway positioning steps — this newborn is well within that window and should move toward PPV rather than continued stimulation alone. Compressions and epinephrine both come later, gated by the response to effective ventilation.

quiz.q: A newborn receives 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation and the heart rate remains at 48. What is the correct next step and ratio?
choices: Continue ventilation alone for another 30 seconds before deciding
Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilation at a 3:1 ratio
Begin compressions alone with no ventilation
Give epinephrine before starting compressions
quiz.why: A heart rate that stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation triggers compressions at a 3:1 ratio (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute), coordinated rather than continued ventilation alone. Compressions are always paired with ventilation in the newborn algorithm, and epinephrine is reserved for continued bradycardia despite compressions and ventilation.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old is found with cool extremities, delayed capillary refill of 3.5 seconds, and tachycardia, but a blood pressure that reads within normal limits for age. How should this be classified?
choices: A normal finding for an anxious child in the emergency department
No shock present, since the blood pressure is normal
Compensated shock — the child is maintaining pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction despite poor perfusion
Hypotensive shock, since the child is clearly decompensating
quiz.why: Compensated shock is defined by signs of poor perfusion — tachycardia, delayed refill, cool extremities — with a blood pressure the child is still maintaining through compensatory mechanisms; waiting for hypotension means waiting for decompensation, which is late. Dismissing the findings as normal or anxiety-related ignores the perfusion signs that are the whole point of recognizing this stage early.
